infrastructure.history: Formerly LAPTEL. The Brazilian laboratory has carried three names. It began as LAPTEL, the Signal Processing and Telecommunications Laboratory; became NIPS, the Centre for Instrumentation and Signal Processing; and took the name NIPS-CERN when the CERN collaboration was formalised and the group gained its second laboratory, at Route Salam in Meyrin. In Brazil the group works from the PPEE building, home of the Graduate Program in Electrical Engineering at UFJF.

pulse.title: What a collision looks like to the electronics
pulse.lede: A cell of the calorimeter answers a particle with one shaped pulse, and the readout keeps seven samples of it. Everything the laboratory builds lives inside this picture.
pulse.source: Reference pulse shape from the ATLAS Collaboration, redrawn from published landmarks and tabulated at 1 ns. The sample values follow from it; they are not measured ADC counts.
pulse.s1: The front-end shapes the cell's signal into a pulse of fixed width, the same shape every time, whatever particle made it. Its height is the energy that was deposited.
pulse.s2: The pulse is digitised at 40 MHz and the readout keeps seven samples. This is the entire record of the event in that cell: seven numbers, and the height has to be found among them.
pulse.s3: Bunches cross every 25 ns, so the next collision arrives before this pulse has finished. Its signal rides on the same window, and the seven samples are no longer the pulse: they are the sum. This is pile-up, and it gets worse with luminosity.
pulse.s4: The amplitude is recovered by a weighted sum of the samples, with the weights computed so that the answer is right despite the deformation. It runs in an FPGA, in real time, for ten thousand channels at once. Optimal filtering, deconvolution and neural estimators for this problem are what the group's twenty years of papers are about.

what_is_cern.title: What is CERN?
what_is_cern.text: Founded in 1954, CERN — the European Organization for Nuclear Research — is the world's foremost laboratory for particle physics. Located on the Franco-Swiss border near Geneva, it brings together more than 17,500 people of some 110 nationalities, with 25 Member States and 11 Associate Member States, Brazil among them. CERN's mission is to push the boundaries of human knowledge by probing the fundamental structure of matter and energy.

lhc.title: The Large Hadron Collider
lhc.subtitle: The most complex machine ever built
lhc.text: Buried between 45 and 170 metres under the Swiss and French countryside, the Large Hadron Collider accelerates protons to within a hair's breadth of the speed of light before smashing them together at four collision points. Each collision recreates conditions that existed a fraction of a second after the Big Bang.

atlas.name: ATLAS
atlas.desc: A Toroidal LHC Apparatus — the largest general-purpose detector, designed to study the full range of particle physics including Higgs searches and BSM physics.

cms.name: CMS
cms.desc: Compact Muon Solenoid — complementary to ATLAS with a different technical design; together they confirmed the Higgs boson in 2012.

alice.name: ALICE
alice.desc: A Large Ion Collider Experiment — studies quark-gluon plasma produced in heavy-ion collisions to understand the early universe.

lhcb.name: LHCb
lhcb.desc: Large Hadron Collider beauty — specialised in CP violation and matter-antimatter asymmetry using B meson decays.

atlas.title: Inside the ATLAS Detector
atlas.subtitle: A layered onion of subdetectors — 46 metres long, 25 metres tall, weighing 7,000 tonnes

inner.name: Inner Detector
inner.desc: Tracks charged particle trajectories using pixel sensors, silicon strips, and transition radiation tracking within a 2 T solenoidal magnetic field.

lar.name: LAr EM Calorimeter
lar.desc: Liquid argon electromagnetic calorimeter measures energy of electrons and photons with an accordion-shaped lead absorber structure.

tile.name: TileCal Hadronic Calorimeter
tile.desc: Scintillating tile calorimeter measures hadronic jet energy. The NIPS-CERN team makes direct contributions to TileCal operations and calibration.

hec.name: Hadronic Endcap (HEC)
hec.desc: Liquid argon hadronic endcap calorimeter covering the forward region, complementing TileCal for full calorimetric coverage.

muon.name: Muon Spectrometer
muon.desc: The outermost layer — a toroidal magnetic system with drift tube chambers tracks muons over the detector's full acceptance.

trigger.title: The Trigger System
trigger.text: The LHC produces 40 million bunch crossings per second. ATLAS cannot record every event — it would produce 60 petabytes of data per second. The trigger system uses two stages: a hardware Level-1 trigger reduces the rate to 100,000 events/s, and a software High-Level Trigger further reduces it to 1,000 events/s — those most likely to contain interesting physics.

nipscern_contribution.title: NIPS-CERN's Contribution to ATLAS
nipscern_contribution.text: Our laboratory contributes to ATLAS through three main pillars: CGV-WEB provides worldwide access to calorimeter event visualisation; SAPHO accelerates hardware prototyping for detector electronics; and our scientific computing team participates directly in data analysis and simulation workflows alongside CERN scientists.

wz.title: W and Z Bosons Discovered
wz.desc: UA1 and UA2 experiments at the SPS collider confirm the carriers of the weak force. Nobel Prize 1984.

web.title: The World Wide Web Invented
web.desc: Tim Berners-Lee proposes an information management system at CERN. The web is born as a scientific tool.

antiH.title: Antihydrogen Created
antiH.desc: LEAR produces the first atoms of antihydrogen — the antimatter counterpart of the simplest atom.

higgs.title: Higgs Boson Discovered
higgs.desc: ATLAS and CMS jointly announce the discovery of the Higgs boson. Nobel Prize awarded 2013 to Higgs and Englert.

run3.title: Run 3 at 13.6 TeV
run3.desc: The LHC begins its third run at record 13.6 TeV centre-of-mass energy, opening a new frontier of precision physics.

projects.title: Our Projects
projects.subtitle: From processor design tools to calorimeter visualisation — each project serves real scientific and engineering needs.

sapho.name: SAPHO
sapho.short: Design a processor, compile for it, simulate it, put it on an FPGA. One toolchain for the whole path.
sapho.desc: SAPHO is a complete hardware architecture and toolchain designed for processor creation, experimentation, and hardware–software co-design. It bundles together the YANC compiler toolchain, the AURORA IDE, the Surfer waveform viewer, and the PRISM RTL Viewer for processor circuit visualisation.

features.title: What SAPHO Includes
features.prism: PRISM RTL Viewer for processor visualisation

yanc.name: YANC
yanc.short: Takes C± or C++ down to assembly, to synthesizable Verilog, to memory images and a testbench.
yanc.desc: YANC is the compilation backbone of SAPHO, bridging high-level processor description languages and low-level execution. It comprises cmmcomp — the CMM language compiler — and asmcomp — the assembly compiler — along with auxiliary tools for the full compilation pipeline.

features.title: Toolchain Components
features.tech: Written in C with Flex, Bison, and GCC
features.integration: Fully integrated into the SAPHO ecosystem

hits.name: HITS
hits.short: Reproduces the ATLAS Tile Calorimeter readout in real time, on an FPGA, at the detector clock.
hits.desc: HITS is a real-time FPGA simulator of the ATLAS Tile Calorimeter readout. It runs at 40 MHz on a Terasic DE10-Nano and rebuilds the front-end signal chain in synthesizable Verilog: pseudo-random hits following the LHC bunch-train structure, energy amplitudes drawn from measured distributions, electronic noise, analog shaping and an embedded pole-zero cancellation. It lets the group validate online energy-reconstruction without access to the experiment.

polaris.name: POLARIS
polaris.short: Modern, lightweight IDE built with Tauri and Rust for the SAPHO ecosystem.
polaris.desc: POLARIS was a cross-platform graphical IDE for the SAPHO ecosystem, built with Tauri and Rust, with Monaco Editor, the PRISM RTL viewer and the YAWT wave tracer. It is archived; AURORA is the current IDE for SAPHO.

features.title: Key Features
features.tauri: Built with Tauri + Rust — lightweight and fast
features.monaco: Monaco Editor (same engine as VS Code)

aurora.name: AURORA
aurora.short: The desktop environment where SAPHO is used: write, build, simulate and read waveforms in one place.
aurora.desc: AURORA is the desktop IDE for the SAPHO platform. You describe a processor in C±, then compile, simulate and inspect it without leaving the window: Monaco editor, Icarus Verilog and Verilator simulation, Surfer, and the PRISM RTL viewer. Aurora Intelligence adds an AI assistant that drives the IDE through its own tools.

cgv.name: CGV-WEB
cgv.short: The calorimeter event display for ATLAS, running in a browser. 186,000 cells at interactive rates.
cgv.desc: CGV-WEB is the online evolution of CaloGeoView, a tool originally developed as part of the PhD thesis of Dr. Luciano Manhães de Andrade Filho. It renders CERN calorimeter events in 3D, colour-coding each detector cell by energy deposit, giving physicists a powerful visual tool for understanding collision data.

privacy.title: Privacy Policy
privacy.subtitle: How we handle information when you visit the NIPS-CERN website.
privacy.highlight: We do not sell data, run advertising, or use tracking cookies. This is a non-commercial academic research website, and what it does keep is listed below.
privacy.s1_body: This privacy policy applies to nipscern.com, operated by NIPS-CERN, the Center for Instrumentation and Signal Processing. The group works from two laboratories: NIPS, at UFJF, in Juiz de Fora, Brazil, and Route Salam, at CERN, in Switzerland.
privacy.s2_body:
Nothing on this site asks who you are. There is no account, no login, and no registration or contact form. Two things still leave your browser, and both are set out below.

Analytics (GoatCounter): We use GoatCounter to count page visits and understand traffic patterns. GoatCounter:

  • Does not use cookies.
  • Does not collect personally identifiable information (no name, email, or device fingerprint).
  • Records only aggregated counts: page URL, referrer, browser family, country (derived from anonymised IP; the full IP address is never stored), and screen size category.
  • Is fully GDPR-compliant and requires no cookie consent banner.

You can review GoatCounter's own privacy policy at goatcounter.com/help/privacy.

Hearts on news posts. Pressing the heart on a post sends a request to a small service of ours running on Cloudflare Workers. It stores a count per post, and one row per post and device to keep the same device from voting twice. The device is written as SHA-256(IP address | browser string | secret salt): the address itself is never stored and the hash cannot be turned back into one. Nothing is stored if you do not press the heart.
privacy.s3_body:
This website keeps three first-party cookie-equivalents, all of them localStorage keys and all of them in your browser: nipscern_lang holds your chosen language, nipscern_anim holds whether you asked for the animations on the projects grid to run, and nipscern:hearts:liked holds the news posts you have marked, so the heart stays filled when you come back.

We do not use advertising cookies, tracking cookies, or third-party analytics cookies.
privacy.s4_body:
The following external services are loaded when you visit this website. Each has its own privacy policy.

  • GitHub: project links point to github.com. GitHub's privacy practices apply when you navigate to those pages. See GitHub Privacy Statement.
  • CERN Courier: PDF links point to cerncourier.com, operated by CERN. CERN's privacy practices apply.
  • Cloudflare: the heart on a news post is counted by a small service of ours running on Cloudflare Workers, and the site's heavier files are served from cdn.nipscern.com. Cloudflare sees those requests the way any host sees a request. See the Cloudflare privacy policy.
privacy.s5_body:
GoatCounter keeps aggregated counts and nothing that points at a visitor, so there is no individual record there to remove.

The hearts table keeps one row per post and device for as long as the count stands. The device is written as a hash, and a hash cannot be worked back to a person, which also means we cannot pick out one reader's row on request. Clearing nipscern:hearts:liked in your browser clears your side of it.
privacy.s6_body: Under the Brazilian Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados (LGPD) and the European General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), you have rights of access, correction and deletion over personal data held about you. What we hold ourselves is set out in sections 2 and 5, and none of it is tied to a name or an account. Those rights apply to anything processed by the third-party services listed above, and to us: write to us and we will answer.
privacy.s7_body: This website is intended for university students, researchers, and the general public interested in particle physics. We do not knowingly collect information from children under 13.
privacy.s8_body: We may update this privacy policy from time to time. The date of the most recent update appears at the top of this page. Continued use of the website after changes are posted constitutes acceptance of the revised policy.
privacy.s9_body: Questions about this privacy policy can be directed to the NIPS-CERN group. See the About page for contact information.

credits.title: Open Source Credits
credits.subtitle: This website is built on the shoulders of great open source projects. We are grateful to the developers and communities behind each of the following libraries, fonts, and services.
credits.projects_intro: The following research software developed by NIPS-CERN is featured on this website and is available as open source.
credits.threejs_desc: 3D WebGL rendering library. It draws the CGV calorimeter visualisation (TileCal barrel, LAr barrel, HEC endcaps) and the coauthorship network on the About page.
credits.gsap_desc: Animation engine behind the scroll choreography on the home page. Free for commercial use, plugins included, since Webflow released the whole library in April 2025.
credits.lenis_desc: Smooth scrolling, on every page. It runs off the same frame clock as the animations that read the scroll position, which is what the browser's own smoothing could not do. By darkroom.engineering.
credits.cern_photos_desc: The aerial view of the Meyrin site, the Globe, the LHC tunnel and its dipole magnet, the ATLAS cutaway and layer diagram, the TileCal module, the LAr accordion, the control room, the trigger chain and the FCC concept. Source: CERN, used for educational and informational purposes under the Terms of Use for CERN Audiovisual Media.
credits.mural_photo_desc: The second stop of the descent on the CERN page. The mural on the building is ATLAS, painted in 2010 by Josef Kristofoletti at half the scale of the detector below it. Photograph from Wikimedia Commons, dedicated to the public domain.
credits.sm_diagram_desc: The particle table on the CERN page. Drawn for Wikimedia Commons and released to the public domain by its author.
credits.osm_desc: The ground drawn over the LHC in the CERN page hero: the France–Switzerland border and the watercourses of the Meyrin countryside, fetched once by tools/build-meyrin-map.js and committed as data. © OpenStreetMap contributors, under the Open Database License.
credits.exp_logos_desc: The marks of ATLAS, CMS, ALICE and LHCb on the map pins of the CERN page hero, identifying each experiment at its interaction point. Each logo belongs to its collaboration and is used whole and unmodified, as their design guidelines require.
credits.pulse_desc: The figure on the CERN page. The shaped pulse, its 150 ns width, the seven samples 25 ns apart and the out-of-time signal from the following bunch crossing all come from J. M. de Seixas, on behalf of the ATLAS Collaboration, "The TileCal Energy Reconstruction for LHC Run2 and Future Perspectives". The curve is redrawn from the published landmarks and tabulated by tools/build-tilecal-pulse.js; the sample values follow from it and are not measured ADC counts.
credits.hyg_desc: Hipparcos, Yale and Gliese combined. The sky over the home page is this catalogue drawn as it is: every star down to magnitude 6 at its own position, with its own brightness and its own colour. Taken in the packed form d3-celestial distributes.
credits.sapho_video_desc: The board on the SAPHO project card. Filmed in monochrome and graded here to the project's own gold, on the black the card shares with it.
credits.aurora_video_desc: The northern lights over a pine wood, on the AURORA project card. Cropped, graded and cut into a loop that runs forward then backward, so it turns over without a seam.
credits.ai_video_desc: A robotic hand opening in front of a vintage television, on the Aurora Intelligence card. Cropped from vertical, graded, and cut into a loop that runs forward then backward, so it turns over without a seam.
credits.phosphor_desc: Icon family behind every glyph in the interface. Self-hosted as CSS masks over the current text colour, so only the icons this site uses are shipped.
credits.geist_desc: Primary sans-serif, carrying body text and interface. A contemporary grotesque, kept quiet so it does not compete with the display face. By Vercel.
credits.bodoni_desc: Display serif behind every heading. A didone, with the extreme stroke contrast the style is known for, and an optical size axis that keeps the hairlines fine at large sizes and solid at small ones. By Indestructible Type.
credits.plexmono_desc: Monospace, used for version tags, code, figures and technical labels.
credits.goatcounter_desc: Privacy-friendly web analytics. No cookies, no personal data collected, no cross-site tracking. View counts on the home page are powered by GoatCounter.
credits.sapho_desc: Simple Architecture for Processor Hardware and Organisation — FPGA processor design platform used for teaching digital logic at UFJF.
credits.yanc_desc: Yet Another NIPS-CERN Compiler — CMM-to-assembly and assembly-to-machine-code compiler for the SAPHO architecture.
credits.hits_desc: Real-time FPGA simulator of the ATLAS Tile Calorimeter readout, running on a DE10-Nano board.
credits.aurora_desc: The desktop IDE for SAPHO: write C±, then compile, simulate and inspect in one window, with the Aurora Intelligence assistant.
credits.cgv_desc: Interactive 3D visualisation of the ATLAS calorimeter system (TileCal, LAr barrel, HEC endcaps) built with Three.js and Vite.

hero.label: Questions & Answers
hero.title: The Big Questions, Answered
hero.subtitle: What people ask about CERN, the ATLAS experiment and the NIPS-CERN projects, answered plainly by the lab that lives this work every day.

qa.a1: NIPS-CERN is a research and development group with two laboratories: NIPS, at the Federal University of Juiz de Fora (UFJF), in Brazil, and Route Salam, at CERN, in Switzerland. The work is electronic instrumentation, signal processing, processors, 3D visualisation and machine learning for high energy physics, much of it on the ATLAS experiment. Meet the team and the mission.
qa.q2: How does a Brazilian laboratory collaborate with CERN?
qa.a2: NIPS-CERN contributes to the operation and calibration of the TileCal hadronic calorimeter of the ATLAS detector, develops digital signal reconstruction methods used in event triggering, and builds software such as CGVWeb, which runs on the main wall of the ATLAS Control Room in Geneva. Members of the lab work both at UFJF and on site at CERN; the full story is on our CERN & ATLAS page.
qa.q3: How can I join NIPS-CERN or propose a partnership?
qa.a3: We are hiring: the lab looks for researchers in logic, philosophy, software engineering, the engineering disciplines, programming and design. Companies and institutions interested in building on our work are welcome: our license is open to partnerships. Write to contact@nipscern.com or meet us through the About page.
qa.a4: SAPHO is a scalable hardware architecture and toolchain for creating processors: you describe an algorithm in a few lines of C±, and SAPHO generates a soft-core processor tailored to run exactly that algorithm on an FPGA. The platform is the sum of its parts (SAPHO = AURORA + YANC) and includes Surfer and PRISM.
qa.a5: AURORA is the official desktop IDE of the SAPHO platform: write the algorithm, compile, simulate and inspect the generated processor in a single window. Aurora Intelligence adds an AI assistant that operates the IDE through its own tools.
qa.a6: YANC is the compiler toolchain powering the SAPHO ecosystem, including cmmcomp (the C± compiler) and asmcomp (the assembly compiler). It is written in C with Flex, Bison and GCC.
qa.a7: CGVWeb renders real collision events from the ATLAS calorimeters in 3D, in any browser, with no installation. Built on Rust/WebAssembly and Three.js, it runs on the main wall of the ATLAS Control Room at CERN. Open the live application or read the technical documentation.
qa.a8: HITS is a real-time FPGA simulator of the ATLAS Tile Calorimeter readout. It runs at 40 MHz on a DE10-Nano and reproduces the front-end signal chain in synthesizable Verilog, so online energy-reconstruction can be validated without the experiment.
qa.q9: What is CERN and what does the name mean?
qa.a9: CERN is the world's largest particle physics laboratory. The name comes from the French Conseil Européen pour la Recherche Nucléaire, the provisional council created in 1952 to plan the laboratory; the organisation it founded kept the acronym. Our CERN & ATLAS page tells the story in depth.
qa.a10: CERN sits on the border between Switzerland and France, just outside Geneva, with its main campus in Meyrin. Its accelerators run underground across both countries, including the ring where the team works with the ATLAS experiment.
qa.q11: When was CERN founded, and by whom?
qa.a11: CERN was founded on 29 September 1954 by twelve European countries rebuilding scientific cooperation after the war. Today it counts more than twenty member states, and scientists from every continent, including Brazil, take part in its experiments.
qa.a12: ATLAS is the largest general-purpose particle detector at the Large Hadron Collider: 46 metres long, 25 metres tall, about 7,000 tonnes, sitting 100 metres underground. In 2012, ATLAS and CMS announced the discovery of the Higgs boson. NIPS-CERN contributes to its TileCal calorimeter; see how.
qa.q13: Where is the LHC, and how does it work?
qa.a13: The Large Hadron Collider is a 27-kilometre ring about 100 metres under the Franco-Swiss border. Superconducting magnets steer two beams of protons travelling near the speed of light into head-on collisions, up to 40 million times per second, recreating conditions close to those of the early universe. Detectors like ATLAS record what comes out.
qa.q14: Which countries and institutions take part in ATLAS?
qa.a14: The ATLAS collaboration gathers thousands of scientists from roughly 180 institutions in around 40 countries. Brazil is among them, and UFJF, through NIPS-CERN, is one of the participating institutions. Our contributions are detailed on the CERN & ATLAS page.
qa.q15: Did CERN open a portal or split a singularity?
qa.a15: No. The LHC collides protons, something cosmic rays do in Earth's atmosphere constantly and at even higher energies, and no portal, dimension or singularity is involved. What the collisions actually produce is far more interesting: precise measurements of the particles and forces that make up our universe. See what really happens inside ATLAS.
qa.q16: What are the 17 particles of the Standard Model?
qa.a16: The Standard Model describes matter with 17 fundamental particles: six quarks, six leptons (including the electron and the neutrinos), four force-carrying bosons (photon, gluon, W and Z) and the Higgs boson, confirmed at CERN in 2012. There is a full diagram on our CERN & ATLAS page.
qa.a17: The CERN Courier is the international journal of high energy physics, published since 1959. NIPS-CERN curates a digital collection of editions from 2013 to today, alongside our own scientific publications.
